 AN CHÚIRT UACHTARACH 

 THE SUPREME COURT 

   

 Supreme Court Appeal Number: S:AP:IE:2024:000124 

 [2026] IESC 2 

   

   

 Dunne J. 

 Charleton J. 

 Hogan J. 

 Murray J. 

 Collins J. 


   

   

 BETWEEN/ 

   

   

 G.M. 

   

 APPLICANT/APPELLANT 

   

  AND  

   

   

   

 I.M. 

   

 RESPONDENT 

   

  AND  

   

   

   

 THE ATTORNEY GENERAL 

   

 NOTICE PARTY 

   

 

 

 JUDGMENT of Mr. Justice Brian Murray delivered this 23 rd day of January 2026 

 1.       I agree generally with the judgment of Dunne J. and adopt her comprehensive account of the facts and arguments of the parties.  However, two issues that appear to me to be of some general importance are touched on in that judgment, and in those of Collins and Hogan JJ.  The first arises from the suggestion that there are necessary geographical limitations on the scope of an Isaac Wunder order made by the District Court or by the Circuit Court.  The second depends on the precise legal basis on which the High Court enjoys the power to make such orders preventing persons from instituting proceedings before the District Court or Circuit Court save with the permission of the Presidents of those Courts. 

   

 2.       In examining each of these questions, it must be remembered that the description " Isaac Wunder Order " can refer to a range of different types of constraint that may be imposed by a court on the ability of a party to institute legal proceedings.  Those restrictions fall into two broad but overlapping categories.  First, a court may make an order in the course of, or at the conclusion of an action restraining one of the parties - usually the claimant - from pursuing an action against the other party save with the consent of a judge (usually the President of the court in question).  That order may be made at the request of one of the parties, but it may also be made by the court sua sponte.  Such an order is made in the exercise of the court's power over its own procedures and to protect the interests of parties before it.  But second, some courts may also make orders restricting a named person from pursuing proceedings in any court, and/or from pursuing any proceedings against any person and/or from pursuing such proceedings of a particular kind.  Orders of this kind may also be made during or at the conclusion of a case before the court, but it is possible that they may be sought in free-standing legal proceedings.  In this second category of case, the court is not necessarily simply exercising a power required for the purposes of protecting its own processes or the rights of identified litigants before it harried by the person the subject of the order.  Instead, it may be asserting a more general jurisdiction in the sense of an authority to take seisin of and determine a cause affecting the right of a person to institute proceedings in another court, and/or to protect the interests of a range of persons who may not necessarily be before it at all (and see in this regard my judgment in Kirwan v. Connors [2025] IESC 21 at paras. 19-20). 

   

 3.       Insofar as the first of these categories is concerned, there is and can be no doubt but that every court by reason of its status and function as such, has the power to control its own proceedings, to prevent the abuse thereof and to adopt measures to limit the capacity of persons to institute vexatious litigation in that court to the detriment of both the court, and other litigants.  The implication of such a power is permissible because it is necessary for the discharge by such a court of its functions in the administration of justice and in the vindication of the rights of those who are brought as defendants before it (see, in particular, the explanation in Riordan v. Ireland (No. 4) [2001] 3 IR 365 , 369).  It is clearly critical to the administration of justice that all courts have the power to restrain abuses of their own processes.  It follows that each court must have the power to restrain the institution of vexatious litigation before it, and for that purpose to condition the bringing of any action by a person who has proven themselves in the past to be a vexatious litigant. This has been well-established since the decision in Grepe v. Loam (1887) 37 Ch D 168 and was a feature of the judicial function when the Constitution was adopted.  The description in the judgment of Abbott J. in SP v. UG [2016] IEHC 693 (at para. 22) is accurate and apt: ' [t]he source of such power to make an Isaac Wunder order comes from the implied power that arises from the duty of all courts to supervise and control their own procedures so as not to be oppressive or to allow parties to be endlessly subject to vexatious applications and litigation being repeatedly brought before the courts.'  Insofar as this power arises where a court restrains vexatious litigation before that court alone, this power necessarily follows from the provisions of Article 34.1 of the Constitution. 

   

 4.       As Walsh J. stressed in the course of his judgment in The State (Boyle) v. Neylon [1986] IR 551, 554-555, it is quite clear from the provisions of the Courts (Establishment and Constitution) Act 1961 that there is only one District Court and only one Circuit Court in the State, the respective jurisdictions of which are exercised on a local basis in accordance with statute.  When a District Court judge or Circuit Court judge discharges their functions in the administration of justice, they accordingly do so as judges of those courts, not as judges only of a particular District or Circuit.  It must follow that their ability to restrain abuses of process is rooted in the power to restrain abuses of the processes of their respective courts, not just of the court when sitting in that District or Circuit.  That is a power that is vested for the protection of the processes not only of the judge and not only of their District or Circuit, but of those of the court of which they are a judge.  It is a power, it should be emphasised, that these courts enjoy as a matter of law because it is necessary to the exercise of their primary function in the due administration of justice.  

   

 5.       The basis for the suggestion that this power is limited by District or Circuit lies in the fact that these are courts of local and limited jurisdiction and, it has been proposed, it follows that there must be some constraint on the reach of such orders, or at least that in implying the power to impose these restrictions on the power of a District or Circuit Court judge, a limitation of this kind should be inferred.  However, it is necessary to be clear about the difference between the jurisdiction of these courts (which must, indeed, be both limited and local), and the geographical extent of orders that may be made by judges of those courts in cases in which they have properly assumed jurisdiction (which need not be local).  As explained in Hosie v. Lawless [1927] IR 464, 471 the policy of the Courts of Justice Act 1924 (" the 1924 Act ") in first establishing such courts was the decentralisation of jurisdiction.  It was not the imposition of a limitation on the reach of orders made by such courts when jurisdiction was properly assumed. In other words, while there must be a limitation on jurisdiction, once jurisdiction has been correctly invoked, and once that jurisdiction is itself limited and local, there is no requirement imposed by the Constitution or anywhere else that orders made by a court of limited and local jurisdiction must themselves be local in scope or effect.  That conclusion simply does not follow from the premise. What does follow from the various jurisdictions conferred by law upon these courts is that in a case in which the Circuit Court (and in this respect the same applies to the District Court) properly has jurisdiction by reference to the statutory constraints of limitation and locality, and in which it is otherwise appropriate for that court to make an order preventing the plaintiff in question from proceeding to unconditionally litigate, as against a particular defendant before the Court, then that order is effective as against that litigant, and can to that extent prevent them from instituting proceedings captured by the order before the Circuit Court anywhere in the State.  An Isaac Wunder order of this kind, it must be stressed, is an in personam order, directed not to any court but to the particular litigant against whom it is made. 

   

 6.       I do not see anything in the judgments in Grimes v. Owners of SS Bangor Bay [1948] IR 350 (" Grimes ") or in Permanent TSB plc v. Langan [2017] IESC 71 , [2018] 1 IR 375 (" Langan ") that suggests otherwise. In Grimes , the issue was whether s. 48 or s. 51 of the 1924 Act could be construed so as to allow the Circuit Court to entertain a claim in rem in Admiralty for wages and wrongful dismissal.  It was clear that the legislation conferred no such express power, being restricted (as was found to be the case) to in personam claims in contract and tort, those jurisdictions in turn being conditioned by monetary and geographical limits.  The party seeking to assert jurisdiction thus had to resort to the contention that that court had been invested with jurisdiction to hear all civil cases that had not been expressly excluded by the 1924 Act, in rem actions in Admiralty not having been so excluded.   That argument was rejected, because if correct it would have meant that the court was invested with jurisdiction to hear cases without any limitation of locality or otherwise.  The ratio of the decision is found in the judgment of O'Byrne J. (with whom Maguire CJ, Murnaghan and Geoghegan JJ. agreed) at p. 355 of the report: a statutory provision that gave general jurisdiction to the Circuit Court in all civil cases subject only to express limitations and exclusions would not be conferring a jurisdiction that was limited and local and would, accordingly, be invalid. 

   

 7.       In Langan , the question was whether the Circuit Court had jurisdiction to entertain possession proceedings in cases where the property in question was shown to have no rateable valuation.  The issue arose in a context in which the relevant provisions of the Courts (Supplemental Provisions) Act 1961 (" the 1961 Act ") restricted Circuit Court jurisdiction over such claims geographically (by, essentially, restricting such claims to the Circuit Court in which the property was located), and limited them to proceedings in which the rateable valuation of the property did not exceed stated amounts.  That presented a net question of construction: did the Schedule to the 1961 Act mean that it was only if the property (a) had a rateable valuation, (b) that was at or below the stated level, that the Circuit Court had jurisdiction (in which case the absence of any rateable valuation was fatal to jurisdiction) or did it mean that the court had jurisdiction unless there was a rateable valuation that exceeded a particular amount (in which case it had jurisdiction where there was no such valuation at all)?  The court having settled on the latter  literal - construction, the question arose whether this meant that there was no limitation on the jurisdiction for such claims (in which case the suggestion was that the relevant provisions of the 1961 Act would be unconstitutional or would fall to be reinterpreted in the light of the double construction rule).  That, in turn, depended on the meaning of the word ' limited ' as it appeared both in the 1961 Act, and in the Constitution. 

   

 8.       Clarke CJ, delivering the unanimous judgment of the court, found the constitutional argument to be misconceived.  In requiring a ' limitation ' on the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court, the Constitution enabled a limitation to particular types of proceeding where the category was not excessively broad or unlimited (which, it was found, was not the case in respect of the category of properties that had no rateable valuation). While the decision in Grimes is not mentioned in Langan, it was the subject of considerable debate in the course of the hearing of that case (as it had informed the decision of the Court of Appeal [2016] IECA 229 , which had arrived at the contrary conclusion).  However, the view adopted by this court in Langan seems to me to be entirely consistent with the decision in Grimes , which was to the effect that because it was constituted as a court of local and limited jurisdiction, the Oireachtas could not give general jurisdiction to the Circuit Court in all civil cases subject only to express limitations and exclusions.  Far from being in tension with Langan , the conclusion in Grimes reflects what the court decided in Langan ; the provision in issue in Langan did not confer a jurisdiction in all civil cases subject to limitations and exclusions, only a jurisdiction in those cases involving either a rateable valuation below a certain level, or no rateable valuation at all.  The category of cases in Langan was described by Clarke CJ (at para. 75) as ' relatively narrow ', and he specifically said (at para. 74) that ' [a] real meaning must be given to the requirement that the jurisdiction of a court such as the Circuit Court is limited. ' 

   

 9.       This statement of Clarke CJ is important.  It means, in particular, that in any given situation in which a jurisdiction is vested in the District or Circuit Court, that jurisdiction must be confined in some way.  This is often achieved by imposing limitations framed by reference to the monetary value of claims of a particular kind, or by reference to the rateable valuation of affected property, but it cannot be out-ruled that some causes of action and consequent relief, irrespective of any financial ceiling, are of a character that they can never be truly said to be ' limited ' as that term is used in the Constitution (and see, in particular, in this regard the comments of Keane CJ in The People (DPP) v. MS [2003] 1 IR 606 at 618-619).   But neither Grimes nor Langan remotely suggest that where the District or Circuit Court is properly seised of a lis on foot of a jurisdiction that is truly limited and local, that the Constitution or statute impose a constraint on the geographical reach of an in personam order that those courts can make.  

   

 10.   Taking the Circuit Court as an example, the Third Schedule to the 1961 Act as reflected in the Circuit Court Rules envisages a very generous geographical jurisdiction in actions in contract and tort: these may be brought in the circuit where the defendant resides or carries on any business or profession, or (in the case of contract) where the contract was made, and (in the case of tort actions) where the tort was committed.  In the case of either cause of action, the jurisdiction is limited (by a specified monetary amount) and local (in that there must be some connection between either the defendant, or the alleged wrong, and the circuit in which the action is commenced).  Once these requirements are met, there is no further limitation.  In an action in either contract or tort, the Circuit Court is empowered to make orders in personam against the defendant that may either incidentally or directly and by design, restrain them from acting in a particular way outside the circuit in question and, where this happens, the court enjoys full authority to act to enforce its order, irrespective of where an activity in breach of the order takes place. 

     

 11.   As I have already observed, orders of the kind in issue in this case are made in the course of or at the conclusion of, and as an adjunct to, proceedings with which the court is as a matter of jurisdiction, properly seised.  When this occurs, the making of the Isaac Wunder order is ancillary to the jurisdiction exercisable and exercised by the court to hear those proceedings.  For my part, I cannot discern any legal basis for the exercise by the District or Circuit Courts of a jurisdiction to entertain a freestanding application to that effect divorced from a specific case, nor can I see how those courts have the jurisdiction to make more general orders restraining a named person from litigating against the world at large.  In that regard I agree with the judgment of Hogan J..  But, where an Isaac Wunder order in the first category to which I have earlier referred is sought in the Circuit Court in the course of, or at the conclusion of an action, or where the judge determines to assert the power to make such an order sua sponte, the claim that it enjoys jurisdiction to make such an order seems to me beyond doubt having regard to the provisions of s. 22(7) of the 1961 Act, which provides as follows: 

   

 ' (7) Without prejudice to any jurisdiction conferred by the previous subsections of this section, the Circuit Court shall have powers of attachment, garnishee and interpleader, and shall have all powers (including the power to appoint a receiver) ancillary to any jurisdiction exercisable by it. ' 

   

 (emphasis added). 

   

 12.   Similar language appeared in s. 57 of the 1924 Act, and of that and the equivalent of s. 22(7) of the 1961 Act, Fitzgibbon J. said in Sligo Corporation v. Gilbride [1929] IR 351, 368: 

   

 ' The only limitations upon the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court are those expressed or implied in the provisions of the Courts of Justice Act, and, subject to those limitations, the Circuit Court has within its locality all the jurisdiction of the High Court.  In particular, sect. 57 confers on the Circuit Judges "powers of attachment, injunction, garnishee, interpleader and all powers" (not, be it observed, "all other powers") "ancillary to any jurisdiction vested in, transferred to, or exercisable by them" ' . 

   

 (emphasis in original). 

   

 13.   The second of the two issues I identified at the start of this judgment relates to the extent of the High Court's jurisdiction over vexatious litigants.  In this appeal we are concerned only with whether the courts enjoy the power to make, within the rubric of a vexatious claim, an order preventing the plaintiff or applicant in a case from instituting any further proceedings against the defendant or respondent without satisfying the court in which it is sought to bring that action that the proceedings are not an abuse of process.  Once that is understood, I think that the jurisdiction of the High Court to make such an order extending to proceedings before the Circuit and District Courts, is clear. 

   

 14.   For a start, there can be doubt but that it is an actionable tort to institute proceedings that constitute an abuse of process, and it must follow that the High Court has jurisdiction to grant injunctive relief preventing a repetition of that abuse.  There is no reason that that power should be limited to a prohibition on the unconditional institution of proceedings in the High Court alone.  Such an order can also be granted on foot of a contractual obligation not to institute legal proceedings of a particular kind, and there is a substantial body of law confirming the inherent power of the High Court to grant injunctive relief preventing a party from instituting legal proceedings in a foreign jurisdiction (see Lett v. Lett [1906] 1 IR 618), or indeed enabling the staying of proceedings in this jurisdiction because the same action is pending between the same parties before the Courts of another State (see Joseph Murphy Structural Engineers Ltd. v. Manitowac (UK) Ltd. (Unreported, Supreme Court, 30 July 1985)).  Similarly, in none of these situations is there any limitation by reference to the permitted jurisdictional extent of those orders. 

   

 15.   The essential principle governing all of these cases is the same, and was explained in In Re Connolly Brothers Ltd, Wood v. Connolly Brothers Ltd. [1911] 1 Ch 731 .  There, it was found that the High Court could make an order restraining a party to proceedings before that court from litigating in another court an issue arising in the case before the High Court.  This power was found operative in relation to both a court of co-ordinate jurisdiction, and an inferior court.  The High Court, it was found, had the power to grant such relief where it was shown that the proceedings being enjoined were vexatious or oppressive (at p. 747 per Buckley LJ).   That power derived from the inherent jurisdiction (properly so called) of the High Court to prevent the vexing of persons by litigation anywhere and this is how - in the case of orders preventing a person from litigating abroad  it was rationalised by Griffin J. in Joseph Murphy Structural Engineers Ltd. v. Manitowac (UK) Ltd.   There, he cited the judgment of Jessell MR in McHenry v. Lewis (1882) 22 Ch D 397 , who referred to ' the general jurisdiction of the Court to prevent a Defendant being improperly vexed by legal procedure ' (at p. 399).  All of these examples show that this extended jurisdiction to orders restricting the ability of a plaintiff to proceed with litigation in any court. 

   

 16.   In my view, this is sufficient to ground the jurisdiction suggested in the majority judgment.  In framing the inherent jurisdiction of the present High Court, it is right to look to the powers that had been found to inhere in the High Court established by the Judicature Acts.  This is what this Court did in Joseph Murphy Structural Engineers Ltd. v. Manitowac (UK) Ltd. Before independence the High Court enjoyed an inherent jurisdiction to make orders in aid of defendants, and for the purposes of preventing their being vexed by abusive litigation in any jurisdiction, and defendants subject to the risk of vexatious suits thus had the right to petition the High Court for orders to that effect.  The cases make it clear that this jurisdiction extended to enable the making of orders preventing the institution or prosecution of proceedings in all courts.  This was not, it should be said, a jurisdiction recognised only because of a need to protect the court from abuse.  At common law, its justification was rooted firmly in protection of the interests of the defendant in a case before the court.  Thus, the law in 1922 and 1937 was that a defendant who had been subject to repeated abusive proceedings or repeated abusive applications in proceedings, had the right to apply to condition the bringing of such proceedings in any jurisdiction in the future.  There is no reason to conclude that that right was extinguished, or the pre-existing jurisdiction negated following the adoption of either of the Constitutions enacted in those years (see, by way of analogy the comments of Sullivan P. and of Hanna J. as to the derivation of powers to punish for contempt in AG v. O'Kelly [1928] IR 308, 318 and 331).  Nor, I should say, can it be assumed that the decision in Wunder v. Hospitals Trust (1940) Ltd. (Unreported, 11 April 1967) was the first occasion on which that power was exercised in this jurisdiction; the ease with which the court made the order and absence of any cited authority might suggest the invocation of a familiar and well understood power.  Given that the jurisdiction was established by clear authority prior to independence, this would not be surprising. 

   

 17.   Finally, in this regard, I would add that it is neither wrong, nor necessary, that an order of this kind, when made, condition the right to bring proceedings by reference only to obtaining the leave of the President of the District Court or Circuit Court.  I see no reason why, in an appropriate case, it could not be made conditional simply on the permission of the President of the High Court.  That, it seems, is what happened in Shannon v. Moran (Unreported, Supreme Court, 9 December 2004), where the Order referred to ' no proceedings ' in a context that seems to have been intended to include the Circuit Court (although the power of the court to make such an Order was not the subject of any discussion in the judgment). 

   

 18.   For these reasons, it is not necessary here to decide whether the High Court enjoys a more general jurisdiction that is ' protective ' of courts of local or limited jurisdiction, nor does the court have to decide whether the function of the High Court in the administration of justice and its full original jurisdiction as provided for in Article 34.3.1° of the Constitution in itself justifies the creation of such a jurisdiction.  However, insofar as these are touched on in some of the decisions considered in the course of the judgments of Dunne J. and of Collins J., I would say the following. 

   

 19.   First, I do not believe it correct to suggest that the High Court enjoys a general ' protective ' jurisdiction over courts of local and limited jurisdiction.   The jurisdiction exercised by the High Court over courts of local and limited jurisdiction is ' supervisory '.  What is supervised is the legality of the decisions and processes of those courts. As Kennedy CJ put it in The State (Hunt) v. Circuit Judge of the Midland Circuit [1934] IR 196, 212 the authority of the High Court over such bodies is properly described as ' superintending and corrective ' and it is this that was transferred on independence: ' [a] superintending and corrective jurisdiction over Courts of inferior jurisdiction and the Judges thereof is part of the sovereign function of the judicial power conferred by the Constitution upon the Courts of Justice set up by it ' (at p. 210).  This was the ' superintendence and control' the origin and parameters of which were so clearly explained and described by O'Higgins CJ in The State (Abenglen Properties) v. Corporation of Dublin [1984] IR 381 at 392.  The High Court in the exercise of that jurisdiction identifies and rectifies errors before these tribunals and supervises the future conduct of their proceedings by orders of mandamus, remittal or declaratory relief, as appropriate.  The jurisdiction was concerned only with the correction of error by those courts, not with the exertion of a general authority over those perceived to have threatened their processes.  The scope of the supervisory jurisdiction so defined is critical to the procedural autonomy of those courts, which - subject of course to their acting lawfully and within jurisdiction - are masters of their own procedure and process.  Apart from the limited circumstances in which orders of mandamus, remittal or relevant declaratory relief are granted by the High Court because of actual or apprehended illegality, that court has no role in directing the procedures or processes of courts of local and limited jurisdiction, whether it be for their own protection, or otherwise.  The autonomy of those courts, and the independence of their jurisdiction and proceedings from interference by Superior Courts are central features of the court system envisaged by the Constitution and which we have operated since 1924. 

   

 20.   This was most authoritatively asserted by Gannon J. in Clune v. Director of Public Prosecutions [1981] ILRM 17 at p. 20: 

   

 'The courts of limited jurisdiction established by legislation pursuant to constitutional authority in that behalf are not in any sense subject to direction, control or supervision by the superior courts established by the Constitution. ' 

     

 21.   That statement - which appears in a longer passage described by Professor O'Malley as having assumed ' something of a canonical status ' (Thomas O'Malley, The Criminal Process (Round Hall, 2009) at para. 15-03) - has been repeated frequently since, most recently by Finlay Geoghegan J. in the course of her judgment in Kelly v. National University of Ireland [2017] IECA 161 , [2017] 3 IR 237.  While there is no doubt but that viewed literally and in isolation, the statement seems at first sight to be in error because - of course - the High Court does have a jurisdiction to supervise courts of local and limited jurisdiction insofar as it enjoys the authority to correct legal error (and indeed, as Collins J. observes the assertion of any power to make Isaac Wunder orders affecting the District or Circuit Courts might be described as a form of ' direction, control or supervision '  although what is being restricted is the right of the litigant, not the power of those courts).  However, Gannon J. obviously understood the nature of the High Court's supervisory jurisdiction, and indeed said it five sentences later (' [t]he High Court has ... the capacity and authority ... to remedy errors of abuse or excess of jurisdiction by any of such "inferior courts" ').  The point he was making was different and, if I can respectfully say so, quite clear (at p. 20): 

   

 ' The Justice sitting in the District Court has the sole and exclusive authority to control and supervise the conduct of proceedings in his own court within the limits of the jurisdiction conferred upon him.  His independence and authority is secured in his freedom not only from pressures of political or executive nature but also from purported intervention, direction, or control by any superior court.' 

      

 22.   Second, while it has been decided in the United Kingdom that a Divisional Court of the Kings Bench had indeed such a ' protective ' jurisdiction, while some of the English cases cited by Dunne J. and Collins J. root the power of the High Court to impose restrictions on the ability of litigants to institute proceedings before lower courts in that jurisdiction and while that ' protective jurisdiction '  was proposed before this State gained its independence, I do not believe that that general jurisdiction transferred to the High Court on independence or the adoption of the Constitution.  This is because it was based on a conception of the power of the High Court that is wholly foreign to our constitutional system. 

   

 23.   It was, in modern times, most significantly applied in in R. v. Davies [1906] 1 KB 32 (" Davies ") where the court decided that it enjoyed the jurisdiction to attach the publisher of matter tending to interfere with the fair trial of a charge before Petty Sessions.  The court was, it was said, ' the guardian and protector of public justice throughout the kingdom' (at p. 38), and being the ' custos morum' (the guardian of morals) of the subjects of the realm ' wherever it meets with an offence contrary to the first principles of common justice, and of dangerous consequence to the public, if not restrained, will adapt such a punishment to it as is suitable to the heinousness of it ' (at p. 39, citing Hawkins Pleas of the Crown Book 2 c. 3, s. 4).  Thus, the function of superintendence vested in that Court meant that in effecting justice ' if and when the attainment of that end required that the misdeeds of others should be corrected as well as the misfeasances of the inferior Courts themselves ... if others whose conduct tends to prevent the due performance of their duties by those Courts have to be corrected as well as the Courts themselves ' (at p. 43).  Even then, the power was exercisable only where the inferior courts did not enjoy the power to protect themselves (at p. 42). 

   

 24.   It was, throughout the 1920s and 1930s stated and restated with increasing emphasis (if not frustration), that the courts established by the 1922 Constitution were not simply a continuation of the old courts of the preceding regime, ' but new Courts established by the Oireachtas under the authority of the Constitution of the Saorstát ' ( Quinn and White v. Stoke and Quirke [1931] IR 558, 564 per Kennedy CJ).  Whatever the extent of its ' supervisory ' jurisdiction, the High Court was not constituted as the ' custos morum ' of the Saorstát, did not have the exorbitant powers envisaged by that status, and in particular did not enjoy the power to invent new criminal offences or to inflict punishments when it met with offences contrary to the first principles of common justice in the manner proposed in Davies .  This, it should be stressed, is effectively what happened in Davies : the Court of Petty Sessions did not itself enjoy the power to punish for ' scandalising the Court ' and, therefore, if the Kings Bench Division did not have the power to do so, it was not an offence to scandalise an inferior court.  In deciding that the Kings Bench division did have that power, the practical effect of its decision was to create a new offence.  Insofar as the notion of a ' protective ' jurisdiction was first suggested here in the context of a consideration of that case (see the arguments of counsel for the Attorney General in Attorney General v. O'Ryan and Boyd [1946] IR 70, 77), the High Court was, in my view, thus in error in Attorney General v. Connolly [1947] IR 213, 222 and 225 in suggesting that it enjoyed such a generally drawn ' protective ' power.  I note in passing that the majority in The State (DPP) v. Walsh and Conneely [1981] IR 412 (" Walsh ") clearly did not accept the view of O'Higgins CJ in that case that the asserted role of the High Court in ' the protection of justice ' mandated summary trial by the High Court of a constructive contempt of the Special Criminal Court in the teeth of the literal terms of Article 38.5 of the Constitution. 

   

 25.   Third, and following from this, the fact that the courts have, since independence, recognised the jurisdiction of the High Court to punish for constructive contempts arising from proceedings before courts of local and limited jurisdiction (and for that matter, of the Special Criminal Court) does not affect this conclusion. It seems to me to be quite reasonable to accept that the offence having been part of the common law prior to 1922, that the established rule was carried over, without necessarily adopting in full the legal theory that originally animated it.  In that regard it is telling that following the establishment of the new courts in 1924, it was assumed that the High Court did indeed enjoy the power to entertain an application for attachment arising from a publication said to be intended or calculated to interfere with a criminal prosecution before the District Court ( Attorney General v. Cooke [1924] 58 ILTR 157), and the fact of that power being vested in the High Court was confirmed in respect of a publication said to have scandalised the Circuit Court in ex tempore judgments delivered by Maguire P. and Gavan Duffy J.  in Attorney General v. O'Ryan and Boyd [1946] IR 70.  The courts here having thus long recognised these offences, they remained part of the law of the State on the enactment of the Constitution. 

   

 26.   Fourth, nor does a protective jurisdiction of this kind follow from the fact that the courts - the District Court, the Circuit Court, the High Court, the Court of Appeal and this Court - are part of a single constitutional system and administering justice collectively.  As was stressed in Connor v. O'Brien [1925] 2 IR 24, 28, the Courts of Justice Act 1924 delivered a complete scheme of Courts ' comprising four separate but co-related units '.  That separation is enforced by the proper understanding of the High Court's supervisory jurisdiction, that tribunal correcting error and where necessary directing process of inter alia the courts of local and limited jurisdiction.  It seems to me to be undermined by the proposition that the High Court can, in addition, generally act on foot of a broadly drawn power to ' protect ' those courts. 

   

 27.   Finally, and following from this, insofar as the constitutional provisions addressing the administration of justice and the full original jurisdiction of the High Court are concerned, the former of these - of course - provides a legal basis for those powers that are necessary to enable judges to discharge their constitutional functions (see, most recently, the decision in Kirwan v. Connors [2025] IESC 21 and, in particular, the judgment of Hogan J.).  As I have explained, the law recognises and has long recognised the right of a defendant the subject of vexatious litigation to petition the High Court for orders to prevent them from being further vexed by abusive litigation.  That encompasses the power to prevent the institution of proceedings in other courts.  However, while this is convenient and promotes efficiency and consistency across the legal system, it seems to me to be difficult to say that the vesting of such a power in the High Court vis-à-vis proceedings in other courts is ' necessary ' for the administration of justice, given that the courts of local and limited jurisdiction themselves have that power.  Article 34.3.1°, unless it is to be intolerably circular, must be understood not as the basis for inventing new jurisdictions, but conferring on the High Court the power to exercise those previously recognised, or subsequently conferred by law.  Henchy J. was, in my view, entirely correct when he said in RD Cox Ltd. v. Owners of the MV Fritz Raabe (Unreported, Supreme Court, 1 August 1974) (at p. 8) that Article 34.3.1° ' is investitive of jurisdiction, not creative of jurisdiction.  It merely declares an amplitude of original jurisdiction in the High Court to encompass all currently justiciable matters. '
